cards.front: What is the fundamental microscopic origin of the magnetic force experienced by a current-carrying conductor?
cards.back: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor arises from the sum of the Lorentz forces acting on the individual moving charge carriers (e.g., electrons) within the conductor as they drift through the external magnetic field.

cards.front: State the scalar formula for the magnitude of the magnetic force on a straight conductor of length $L$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$.
cards.back: $F = I L B \sin\theta$, where $I$ is the current, $L$ is the length of the conductor segment within the field, $B$ is the magnetic field strength, and $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of the conventional current and the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$.

cards.front: Describe the Right-Hand Rule used to determine the direction of the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor.
cards.back: Align your fingers with the direction of the conventional current ($I$). Curl your fingers towards the direction of the magnetic field ($\vec{B}$). Your thumb will then point in the direction of the magnetic force ($\vec{F}$). This rule applies to positive charge flow.

cards.front: Write the vector form of the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor segment $\vec{L}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$.
cards.back: $\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$, where $I$ is the scalar current, $\vec{L}$ is a vector whose magnitude is the length of the conductor segment and whose direction is the direction of the conventional current, and $\vec{B}$ is the magnetic field vector.

cards.front: A 0.5 m wire carrying 2A is placed in a 0.1T magnetic field. What is the force if the wire is oriented parallel to the field lines?
cards.back: $F = I L B \sin\theta$. If the wire is parallel to the magnetic field, $\theta = 0^\circ$. Since $\sin(0^\circ) = 0$, the magnetic force on the wire is $F = (2 \text{ A})(0.5 \text{ m})(0.1 \text{ T})(0) = 0 \text{ N}$. There is no magnetic force.

cards.front: Derive the formula for the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor, $F = I L B \sin\theta$, starting from the Lorentz force on individual charge carriers.
cards.back: Consider a conductor of length $L$ and cross-sectional area $A$ with $n$ charge carriers per unit volume, each with charge $q$, moving with drift velocity $\vec{v_d}$. The Lorentz force on a single charge carrier is $\vec{f} = q(\vec{v_d} \times \vec{B})$. The total number of charge carriers in the segment $L$ is $N = nAL$. The total force $\vec{F}$ is the sum of these individual forces: $\vec{F} = N \vec{f} = (nAL) q(\vec{v_d} \times \vec{B})$. The current $I$ in the conductor is defined as $I = nAq v_d$. We can define a vector $\vec{L}$ of magnitude $L$ in the direction of conventional current (same as $\vec{v_d}$ for positive charges). Substituting $I$ and $\vec{L}$, we get $\vec{F} = I (\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$. The magnitude is $F = I L B \sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{L}$ and $\vec{B}$.

cards.front: Calculate the magnitude of the force on a 10 cm wire carrying 5 A, placed perpendicular to a 0.2 T uniform magnetic field.
cards.back:
Using the formula $F = I L B \sin\theta$:
Given: $I = 5 \text{ A}$, $L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$, $B = 0.2 \text{ T}$.
Since the wire is perpendicular to the field, $\theta = 90^\circ$, so $\sin(90^\circ) = 1$.
$F = (5 \text{ A})(0.1 \text{ m})(0.2 \text{ T})(1) = 0.1 \text{ N}$.
The magnitude of the magnetic force is $0.1 \text{ N}$.
